title: Superior Oblique Palsy: Unilateral vs. Bilateral Mastery

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Superior Oblique Palsy (SOP) results from dysfunction of the 4th Cranial (Trochlear) Nerve. It is the most common cause of isolated vertical strabismus in both children and adults. The trochlear nerve is unique: it is the longest CN, the only one to exit dorsally, and the only one to cross the midline completely before exiting the brainstem, making it highly susceptible to trauma.

rows: Reversing HT (RHT in L-gaze, LHT in R-gaze)

sections.title: Clinical Features (Unilateral)
content: Ipsilateral Hypertropia (HT) - worse in contralateral gaze.
Abnormal Head Position: Tilt to contralateral shoulder.
Excyclotorsion (subjective and objective).
Diplopia: Vertical and torsional, worse in downgaze.
Facial Asymmetry: Often seen in congenital cases (ipsilateral cheek fullness).

sections.title: The 'Masked' Bilateral SOP Red Flags
content: Traumatic origin (even mild head injury).
Excyclotorsion > 10 degrees on Double Maddox Rod.
Reversing Hypertropia on side-to-side gaze.
Significant V-pattern esotropia in downgaze.
Minimal Hypertropia in primary position despite large tilt test results.

sections.title: Diagnostics: Parks-Bielschowsky 3-Step Test
content: Step 1: Determine which eye is higher in primary position (e.g., Right Hypertropia).
Step 2: Determine if HT increases in Right or Left gaze (e.g., RHT increases in Left Gaze).
Step 3: Determine if HT increases on Right or Left head tilt (e.g., RHT increases on Right Tilt).
Conclusion: If all three correlate, positive for isolated cyclovertical muscle palsy (Right SO in this example).

rows: Weakening of ipsilateral IO AND contralateral IR
SO tuck + IO weakening + contra IR recession
Harada-Ito or Bilateral SO tuck/IO weakening
Exploration of the SO and tendon

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Slit-lamp: Usually normal.
Gonioscopy: Not routinely indicated unless trauma/glaucoma suspected.
Fundoscopy: Look for excyclotorsion (fovea below the base of optic nerve).
Lancaster Red-Green: Shows the torsional and vertical deviation profile.
Prism Under Cover Test: Measurement in 9 cardinal positions.

sections.title: Advanced Imaging & Workup
content: MRI Brain/Orbits: Thin-cut T1 images to look for SO muscle belly atrophy (congenital).
MRA/CTA: Indicated if associated with other CN palsies (rule out aneurysm).
Blood Work: HBA1c, Blood Pressure (if microvascular suspected in patients >50).
Tensilon/Ice Test: Only if Myasthenia Gravis is a differential.

content.explanation: Superior muscles are IN-torsionists; Recti muscles are AD-ductors. (Helps determine muscle action during tilt and gaze steps).

sections.title: Management: The Harada-Ito Procedure
content: Indication: Primarily for symptomatic excyclotorsion (Bilateral or Unilateral) without significant vertical deviation.
Step 1: Identify the Superior Oblique tendon.
Step 2: Split the tendon longitudinally, isolating the anterior fibers (responsible for torsion).
Step 3: Displace the anterior fibers anteriorly and laterally (Fells modification).
Step 4: Secure with non-absorbable suture (e.g., 6-0 Mersilene) to the sclera.
Effect: Increases the mechanical advantage of the SO for incyclotorsion.

sections.title: Surgical Hierarchy (Unilateral)
content: Small Deviation (<15PD): Weakening of the ipsilateral IO.
Medium Deviation (15-25PD): IO weakening + Contralateral IR recession.
Large Deviation (>25PD): 3-muscle surgery (SO tuck + IO weakening + Contra IR recession).
SO Laxity: Superior Oblique Tuck (be wary of inducing iatrogenic Brown Syndrome).

sections.title: Landmark Studies & Clinical Pearls
content: PEDIG Studies: Highlight the effectiveness of prisms for small deviations.
The 'Over-Correction' Rule: In traumatic SOP, wait 6-12 months for spontaneous recovery.
Congenital SOP Pearl: Patients often have large vertical fusion amplitudes (>10-15PD), whereas acquired cases have normal amplitudes (1-3PD).
Bilateral Pearl: If you fix one side and a large HT appears on the other, you've 'unmasked' the bilateral palsy.

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
content: Iatrogenic Brown Syndrome: Following SO tuck, look for restricted elevation in adduction.
Overcorrection: Resulting in 'reverse' 3-step test positivity.
Undercorrection: Residual diplopia in downgaze (reading position).
Recurrence: Rare in congenital cases after surgery; more common in traumatic cases due to progressive atrophy.
Prognosis: Excellent with surgery; 80-90% success rate in achieving single binocular vision in primary position.
